transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-02 16:00 PT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (SE), Becca Liu (CSM) — Maya Chen (CTO), Evan Ross (SRE), Liam O'Neill (Product), Priya Desai (Backend)

Summary:
- Quick review of last week's steady-state numbers: average throughput per GPU and intermittent tail latency spikes during burst windows.
- Agreed to run two mixed-workload replays with more realistic concurrency distribution and to collect KV-cache metrics.
- Focus for next week: tune continuous batching window + raise concurrency caps for non-priority endpoints, trial small-batch prefetch for critical flows.

Topics: throughput, continuous batching, concurrency ceilings, queue depth, KV cache hits, fallback models, telemetry

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, uh, great to see you all. Quick readout — we'll do 20 minutes of results and then a tuning playbook, right?
[00:14] Maya: Yeah that's perfect. We want to get the p95 down during our morning surge, that's the main metric internal stakeholders care about.
[00:22] Arjun: Cool. To orient — last week we ran the mixed trace you provided at three concurrency levels: 64, 96, and 128 per node. The best steady throughput was at 96 with continuous batching window set to 12ms. We saw p50 around 60ms but p95 spiked to 820ms during bursts.
[00:40] Evan: Right. The spikes correlate with when a batch composition gets very large — the queue drains then one big batch goes out and it bumps the tail. Also, we noticed K V cash misses — sorry, KV cache misses — in the same windows.
[00:58] Priya: Just to add, our traffic mix has a long-tail of long-context prompts which increases token work per request, so when those show up concurrently it amplifies the queuing.
[01:12] Liam: Are we confident the model variant is the same across all nodes? I remember there was a fallback variant configured in the sandbox.
[01:20] Becca: We validated the model hash earlier; there was one node that pulled the fallback during a capacity hiccup, that may have skewed some metrics.
[01:30] Sofia: Okay, good callout. Action: we'll flag the node and exclude its run from the baseline. But we should also talk knob changes that can reduce the p95 without losing average throughput.
[01:42] Arjun: Two levers we recommend: first, tighten the continuous batching window to 6–8ms for the latency-sensitive endpoints. That reduces batch build-up. Second, set concurrency targets per logical route instead of per-node default — give critical endpoints higher concurrency floor but cap long-context requests with a separate pool.
[02:02] Maya: How much throughput do we lose if we shorten the batching window? Our compute is limited, we don't want to double GPU usage.
[02:08] Arjun: Expect 6–12% drop in tokens/sec for comms that are highly batchable. But you'll see p95 improve by ~30–40% in the traces we ran. The drop depends on request size distribution — with your long-context share it's on the higher end.
[02:26] Evan: Is there an option to do opportunistic batching — like allow longer windows when backlog is low and tighten during surges?
[02:34] Arjun: Yes — we can implement adaptive windowing. Redwood runtime already exposes chaos toggles: adaptive_batch_window=true with thresholds based on queue depth/latency. It's experimental in staging but we've used it in a couple of pilots.
[02:46] Priya: Experimental is fine, as long as we can toggle it quickly and roll back.
[02:50] Arjun: Totally. We'll provide a short runbook for enabling/disabling.
[02:56] Liam: You mentioned separating long-context requests to another pool. How heavy is that to set up?
[03:02] Arjun: Not heavy if you route by header or endpoint — create two worker pools: standard and long-context. Standard gets lower max_seq_len and higher concurrency; long-context gets higher seq cap but lower concurrency. Works with our routing policy and doesn't require infra changes.
[03:16] Maya: Can we back-pressure long-context flows instead of dropping them? We need graceful degradation, not 500s.
[03:22] Sofia: Yes—we recommend graceful queueing + early reject policy for non-critical endpoints. For critical endpoints use a small prefetch batch so you keep latency SLO but sacrifice some throughput if needed.
[03:34] Evan: On the KV cache — Arjun, were the misses due to shard imbalance or eviction?
[03:38] Arjun: A mix. The eviction TTL was short in that run and one of the nodes had slightly higher churn. We'll surface detailed KV metrics: hit rate by key prefix, eviction counts, and per-request KV lookup latency.
[03:50] Priya: If we see hot keys, can we pin them? We have a handful of very common prefixes.
[03:55] Arjun: Yes, hot-key pinning is available; we'll show how to configure pins and expected memory cost.
[04:02] Liam: For concurrency ceilings — what's the recommendation for our size? We have 6 GPUs in staging, similar in prod.
[04:08] Arjun: Start with per-GPU concurrency of 96 for mixed traffic, but route high-QPS endpoints with a target of 160 across the cluster. If you need predictable latency for a given endpoint, bump its per-route concurrency and scale out GPUs or use reserved capacity.
[04:24] Maya: Reserved capacity is the enterprise option but we want to avoid that until we have steady patterns.
[04:30] Sofia: Right — dedicated pools are optional. For the POC let's tune the runtime first. If we can't meet p95 without unacceptable cost, we can discuss reserved nodes.
[04:40] Evan: One more telemetry ask — can Redwood emit queue depth histograms and batch size distribution to our prometheus endpoint? That would help us correlate application-level tracing.
[04:50] Arjun: Yep, we can push metrics via remote write and provide a Grafana dashboard. We'll add queue-depth, batch-size, kv_cache_hit_rate, and model-switch events.
[05:00] Maya: That will help. Also, we'd like a short checklist of what to change during the replay so we can do A/B runs: exact knobs, expected signals.
[05:08] Arjun: We'll prepare that. Suggested A/B: baseline (window 12ms, concurrency 96), A: window 6ms, concurrency 96, B: window 8ms, concurrency per-route caps (critical=160, long-context pool=48).
[05:24] Becca: Also keep a run where adaptive_batch_window is on vs off so you can compare.
[05:29] Priya: For the replays — should I use the sample runner or your replay tool?
[05:34] Sofia: Use your runner but format traces per our template; Arjun will share the small script that converts to the runner format. That avoids transfer of PII.
[05:44] Liam: Any concerns about model fallbacks triggering unexpectedly? I want to ensure we don't silently degrade to a smaller model.
[05:50] Arjun: We'll lock the model pin for the POC runs; fallback only triggers if explicit capacity exhaustion policy is hit. We'll also emit an event if fallback happens.
[05:58] Maya: Good. To recap, we'll run the two replays, Redwood will send the spreadsheet and runbook, and then we'll do a hands-on tuning session next week.
[06:07] Sofia: Yep — action list and dates in the meeting notes. Anything else?
[06:12] Evan: Quick question — differences in quantization between our local builds and Redwood runtime? We saw slightly different latency on the 4-bit model earlier.
[06:20] Arjun: There are micro-ops and kernel selection differences; we can share the model config and quant profile we ran. Usually perf varies 5–10% depending on tensor layout. We'll include that in the spreadsheet.
[06:34] Priya: OK, thanks. Sounds good.
[06:38] Sofia: Great — we'll follow up with links: throughput spreadsheet, KV cache metrics dashboard, runbook and conversion script. Thanks everyone.
[06:46] Maya: Thanks all.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard technical terms ("K V cash" instead of "KV cache"), speaker overlaps near 00:50–01:10.
